BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- A former Colombian congressman who was held hostage in the jungle for more than eight years has escaped -- with the help of a former captor. Oscar Tulio Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. Oscar Tulio Lizcano, his hair disheveled, appeared too weak to stand for long when he met the news media Sunday, hours after stumbling onto a military patrol -- and freedom. Lizcano suffered from hunger and disease in captivity and endured isolation in the company of leftist rebels who often would not let him talk, he and Colombian authorities said. "Maybe my incoherence is for a lack of speaking," Lizcano told reporters. "I was unable to talk with the guerillas who guarded me." Lizcano said he had little to read in the jungle except "The Odyssey" by Homer. He suffered from malaria and other illnesses and once ate nothing but hearts of palm for six or seven days, said Juan Manuel Santos, the Colombian defense minister. "This is big news for the whole family," said Lizcano's sister, Amparo Lizcano. "We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died." The former congressman fled about three days ago with the assistance of one of his captors, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, a leftist rebel force that has been fighting the government for more than 40 years in a war that also has involved right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.  Watch release of FARC hostage » . President Alvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday with the ex-FARC rebel -- known by the alias "Isaza" -- and said the man will receive compensation and permission to resettle in France with his family. He said that's in keeping with a Colombian government policy that rewards rebels who desert and help hostages gain their freedom. Police officers and soldiers pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months ago, Santos said. They monitored the location for about five months and took steps to seal off possible escape routes, he said, as they planned a rescue operation using information gleaned help from a rebel who deserted October 2. Troops started that rescue operation Saturday -- only to discover that "Isaza" and Lizcano had decided on their own to escape. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol Sunday, said Santos, the defense minister. Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. He and his former captor stumbled Sunday onto a patrol near the border of the states of Risaralda and Choco, in central Colombia, authorities said. The FARC holds an estimated 750 hostages in Colombia. Its members have justified hostage taking as a legitimate military tactic. The rebels have been battered this year by government raids that killed several top commanders, the death by apparent heart attack of their founder and a wave of desertions. Government commandoes tricked the FARC in July and freed their most prized hostage, the former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, in an elaborate ruse that also liberated three U.S. defense contractors and 11 other hostages. On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of encouragement to those hundreds who remain trapped in the jungle, captives of the FARC. "Hold on. Hold on," he said. "One day you will enjoy your freedom, too." -- CNN's Karl Penhaul contributed to this report .

For more than eight long years, former Colombian congressman Oscar Tulio Lizcano existed as a ghost in the dense, impenetrable jungles of Colombia. Abducted by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) in August 2000, Lizcano was held as a high-value political hostage, intended to be used as a bargaining chip in the guerrilla group’s decades-long conflict against the state. His ordeal finally came to a dramatic end in October 2008, when a desperate bid for freedom and an unlikely alliance brought one of Colombia’s longest-running captivity sagas to a triumphant close.

Lizcano’s captivity was marked by unimaginable hardship. Forced to live under the suffocating canopy of the jungle, he suffered from severe malnutrition, malaria, and intense psychological torment. Hostages were routinely marched through treacherous terrain for weeks at a time to evade military radar, kept in total isolation from the outside world and their families. As the years dragged on, Lizcano’s health deteriorated rapidly, and to his grieving family back home, his survival felt increasingly miraculous.

The turning point came in late October 2008, not through a high-risk military raid, but through an internal collapse of rebel discipline. A young FARC guard known by the alias "Isaza" (Wilson Bueno Largo), tasked with guarding the ailing politician, reached a breaking point. **Colombian politician escapes FARC after 8 years in jungle captivity**

By **CNN Staff**
October 26, 2008

**(CNN) —** A former Colombian congressman kidnapped by Marxist rebels eight years ago has escaped his captors, trekking through dense jungle for three days alongside a guerrilla deserter to reach freedom, Colombian authorities announced Sunday.

Óscar Tulio Lizcano, 61, was emaciated, bearded, and exhausted when he was received by military forces in the western province of Chocó. He had been held by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as the FARC, since his abduction in August 2000. 

His escape marks another devastating blow to Latin America’s oldest rebel insurgency, which has suffered a series of high-profile military defeats, internal betrayals, and leadership deaths this year.

Speaking to reporters in the city of Cali, a visibly frail Lizcano struggled to find words after years of forced silence and isolation in the jungle. 

"I walked for three days and three nights, dodging FARC security rings, through swamps and rivers," a tearful Lizcano said, wearing an oversized military jacket. "I am free. I feel like I have been reborn."

### A daring escape

According to Colombian Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos, the escape was made possible by a lower-level FARC commander known by the alias "Isaza." 

Santos said Isaza, a member of the FARC’s 57th Front, made the decision to break ranks with the guerrilla group last week. Taking Lizcano with him, the rebel navigated through treacherous jungle terrain while actively hunted by both military forces conducting operations in the area and angry FARC troops seeking to recapture them.

Early Sunday morning, the duo encountered a army patrol. 

"The subversive came out with a white flag, carrying Mr. Lizcano, who was in a state of severe malnutrition and extreme fatigue," Santos told CNN. 

Isaza told reporters he decided to flee because pressure from the Colombian military had left his unit starving and surrounded, and because he wanted a better future for himself and his girlfriend, another rebel who escaped around the same time.

"I decided to bring him out because he was very sick, and I knew the FARC was going to let him die," Isaza said. 

### Uribe offers reward, asylum

President Álvaro Uribe praised the bravery of the military forces operating in the region and moved quickly to capitalize on the escape, offering a reward to the rebel who helped Lizcano.

Speaking from Bogota, Uribe announced that Isaza would receive a cash reward of roughly $400,000 and that the Colombian government would assist him in seeking asylum in France. 

"To the members of the FARC who are thinking of deserting: Do it," Uribe said in a nationally televised address. "Look at Isaza. He brought out a hostage, he is receiving a reward, and he will enjoy freedom in a democratic nation."

Medical officials who examined Lizcano said the former lawmaker was suffering from extreme dehydration, skin lesions, and speech difficulty brought on by severe psychological stress and years with little human interaction. However, doctors confirmed he was in stable condition and expected to make a full recovery.

### FARC in retreat

Lizcano was one of the highest-profile political hostages remaining in FARC hands following the dramatic July rescue of former presidential candidate Íngrid Betancourt and three American contractors in "Operation Jaque."

The FARC, which was founded in 1964 as a Marxist peasant militia, has seen its ranks decimated in recent years by a U.S.-backed military crackdown initiated under President Uribe.

Analysts say Lizcano’s escape highlights the waning discipline and deteriorating morale within the rebel ranks.

"This shows that the FARC’s chain of command is cracking," said Michael Shifter, a senior fellow at the Inter-American Dialogue think tank. "When mid-level commanders decide their best option is to hand over high-value hostages to the state, it signals that the insurgency is losing its grip."

For Lizcano’s family, the political implications mattered far less than the end of an eight-year nightmare. His son, Juan Carlos Lizcano, wept as he embraced his father on live television.

"We never lost faith," the younger Lizcano said. "Today, my family is complete again."

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia (CNN)** — A frail, emaciated former Colombian congressman is safe today after a grueling three-day trek through dense tropical jungle, ending an eight-year hostage ordeal at the hands of Marxist rebels. 

In a dramatic twist that has dealt yet another crippling blow to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Oscar Tulio Lizcano did not escape alone—he was brought out by the very rebel commander assigned to keep him captive.

Lizcano, 61, who was kidnapped by the guerrillas in October 2000, emerged from the rain-soaked wilderness of western Chocó province on Sunday, supported by a 28-year-old FARC fighter known by the alias "Isaza." 

Garbed in a tattered shirt, sporting a long gray beard, and struggling to speak, Lizcano looked visibly exhausted as he was airlifted to a military base in Cali before being taken to a hospital in Bogotá. Yet, despite his extreme physical weakness, his first public words were of profound relief.

### A Captor Turns Savior

The architect of the escape was Wilson Bueno Largo, better known within the FARC ranks as "Isaza," the head of a security ring for the group’s 47th Front. According to military sources, Isaza’s unit had been under relentless pressure from military operations for weeks, encircled and starving.

Fearing for his life and disillusioned with the insurgent movement, Isaza made a daring decision: he would desert, but he would take his high-value prisoner with him to guarantee his own survival and freedom.

For three days and nights, the young rebel and the aging politician slogged through swamps and dense vegetation, dodging both army patrols and FARC kill squads sent to recapture them. Sustaining themselves on wild palm hearts and river water, the duo finally stumbled upon an army outpost.

"We walked until we couldn't walk anymore," Isaza told local reporters, explaining that he took the gamble to build a better future for himself and his girlfriend, who also deserted. "I decided to free Mr. Lizcano because I realized the war was lost, and I wanted to give him back his life."

### Emotional Relief for a Devastated Family

For the Lizcano family, who spent nearly a decade living in the agonizing limbo that defines Colombia’s kidnapping crisis, news of his sudden freedom brought overwhelming tears.

Speaking to CNN from Cali, Oscar’s sister, Amparo Lizcano, struggled to contain her emotions as she described watching television footage of her brother’s return.

"We thought he was going to die in those mountains," Amparo said, her voice trembling. "For eight long years, our family was broken, living with a dark cloud over us every single day. To see him walk out of that jungle—even so thin, even so weak—it is a complete miracle. It feels like watching someone be resurrected."

Amparo also expressed a complex debt of gratitude to the man who had, until recently, been her brother's jailer. 

"Isaza held his life in his hands for a long time," she added. "In the end, he chose humanity over hatred. We forgive him for the past, and we thank God that he found the courage to bring my brother back to us."

### A "Fatal Blow" to the FARC

The escape marks another devastating setback for the FARC, coming just months after the high-profile military rescue of former presidential candidate Íngrid Betancourt and three American contractors in Operation Jaque.

At a news conference in Bogotá, Colombian Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos hailed the escape as a testament to the government’s relentless military pressure and appealed directly to other rebels to lay down their arms.

"This is a fatal blow to the morale of the FARC," Santos declared. "It demonstrates that the rank-and-file guerrillas know the game is up. Their command structure is collapsing, and their own fighters no longer believe in the cause."

Santos confirmed that Isaza would receive a substantial cash reward offered by the government for the release of high-profile hostages, as well as protection under a government program that facilitates asylum in Europe. President Álvaro Uribe has already requested that the French government grant Isaza diplomatic asylum.

"To all remaining FARC fighters, I say this: follow Isaza’s example," Santos urged. "Turn in your weapons, bring out your hostages, and the Colombian state will protect you. The jungle is no longer a safe haven for the FARC."

As Oscar Tulio Lizcano begins the long road to physical and psychological recovery in a Bogotá hospital, his story serves as a stark symbol of Colombia's shifting tide—a nation where the once-feared jungle insurgencies are increasingly unraveling from the inside out.

***

*Lucia Newman, CNN, Bogotá, Colombia.*

* **The Journey:** They trekked through the dense rainforests of the Chocó region for three days with little food until they reached a Colombian military outpost.
* **The Aftermath:** 
  * The Colombian government awarded Isaza a cash reward of approximately $1 billion Colombian pesos (around $450,000 USD at the time).
  * To protect him from FARC retaliation, France granted Isaza a visa, and he relocated there shortly after the escape.
